materials.videoTitle: MIT 18.01SC Session 44: Adding Areas of Rectangles

notes.summary: Integration begins with a geometric question: how do we compute the area under an arbitrary curve? The answer starts crudely — chop the region into rectangles and add their areas. This session shows how sums of rectangle areas approach the true area as the slices narrow, motivating the definite integral before any notation is introduced.
notes.focus: Estimate the area under a curve by hand with 4, then 8, rectangles. Watching the two estimates converge toward each other is the whole idea of the Riemann sum.

notes.summary: Riemann sums formalize the rectangle idea: partition the interval, sample the function, sum the areas, and take the limit as the partition refines. This session makes the definition precise and introduces the integral sign as compressed notation for that limit. The recitation video drills the mechanics of setting up sums for concrete functions.
concepts: The definite integral as a limit
notes.focus: Write one Riemann sum fully in sigma notation before converting to integral notation. Being fluent in both directions is what makes later theorems readable.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

materials.videoTitle: MIT 18.01SC Session 47: Introduction of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

notes.summary: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is the hinge of the subject: it connects derivatives (rates) to integrals (accumulation). This session introduces Part 1 — that integration and differentiation are inverse operations — and shows why evaluating an antiderivative at the endpoints can replace computing a limit of sums. It is the single most important theorem of the term.
concepts: The connection to velocity and distance
notes.focus: After watching, state the theorem in your own words with a velocity/distance example. If you can explain why it is more than a computational shortcut, you have it.

lessons.title: Applications of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

materials.videoTitle: MIT 18.01SC Session 49: Applications of the FTC

notes.summary: This session puts the FTC to work on concrete problems: computing definite integrals from known antiderivatives and reading word problems for the quantity being accumulated. You practice matching a physical quantity (distance, work, area) to the integral that models it, then evaluating cleanly with the theorem.
notes.focus: Solve three integrals start to finish without notes. Speed matters less than writing the correct antiderivative and handling the evaluation bounds carefully.

lessons.title: The Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

materials.videoTitle: MIT 18.01SC Session 51: The Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

notes.summary: Part 2 of the FTC is subtler: it treats the integral itself as a function. Define F(x) as the accumulated area up to x and the theorem says F'(x) = f(x) — differentiation undoes integration. This is the idea that lets you differentiate functions defined by integrals, a construction that appears constantly in probability and physics.
concepts: Why F' = f follows from area
notes.focus: Differentiate a function like x-integral of sqrt(1+t^3) dt with the theorem, not by evaluating. Then check your answer with the chain rule version that includes an inner function.

materials.videoTitle: MIT 18.01SC Session 59: Volume of a Parabaloid, Revolving About y-axis

notes.summary: Slicing generalizes from area to volume: revolve a curve, add up disks or shells, and an integral produces the volume. This session works a full example (a paraboloid about the y-axis) and teaches the decision that students find hardest — when to slice into disks versus cylindrical shells, and how to set up the bounds either way.
notes.focus: Take one region and compute its volume twice: once with disks, once with shells. Getting the same number two ways is the strongest possible check on your setup.

notes.summary: Some integrals only yield when you trade x for a trig identity: sqrt(1-x^2) begs for sine, sqrt(1+x^2) for tangent. This session covers the three standard trig substitutions and the back-substitution step, alongside the sin/cos power integrals from session 68 (the reading) that supply the identities you need.
concepts: When NOT to use trig sub
notes.focus: Build a reference card: which radical pairs with which substitution. Then work one full problem and draw the triangle you use to return to x.

notes.summary: Rational functions integrate nicely after you split them: partial fractions decomposes P(x)/Q(x) into simple terms whose antiderivatives are logarithms and arctangents. This session covers the advanced cases — repeated factors and irreducible quadratics — with the basic setup (session 74) as reading. The technique is pure algebra, which makes it very mechanical once the pattern is set.
notes.focus: Do one decomposition with a repeated factor end to end. Check your coefficient algebra by plugging in a convenient value of x before integrating.

notes.summary: Integration by parts is the product rule run backwards, and it is the technique of last resort for integrals like x*e^x or ln(x). This session derives the formula, teaches the u/dv choice heuristic (choose u by LIATE), and shows repeated applications and the classic boomerang case where the original integral reappears and you solve for it algebraically.
concepts: The boomerang integral: e^x sin x
notes.focus: Integrate e^x sin(x) twice and watch the original integral come back. Solving for it algebraically feels like a trick the first time and a tool every time after.

notes.summary: What is the area under a curve that never ends? Improper integrals extend the definite integral to infinite bounds and to unbounded functions by taking limits. Some converge to finite values and some diverge — the p-integral family (1/x^p) is the reference chart for deciding. L'Hopital's rule (reading) supplies the limit tooling this unit leans on.
notes.focus: For the integral of 1/x^p from 1 to infinity, work out the convergence condition yourself with a limit. One number, p=1, divides two very different worlds.

notes.summary: Taylor series express a function as an infinite polynomial built from its derivatives at one point. This session constructs the series for e^x, sin, and cos, and shows how the partial polynomials approximate the function better and better. Combined with infinite series convergence (session 94, the reading), this is the grand payoff of the whole calculus sequence.
concepts: Series for e^x, sin x, cos x, 1/(1-x)
notes.focus: Derive the Maclaurin series for sin(x) yourself from the formula, then compare its 3-term polynomial against a calculator for small x. Approximation quality near the center point is the pattern to remember.

notes.summary: Checkpoint on the middle of the course: the definite integral, the FTC, volumes, and the full toolbox of techniques (substitution, trig, parts, partial fractions). Work the Unit 3 and 4 exam problems under time pressure before reading any solutions. Your technique-chooser — which method for which integrand — is the skill being tested.
notes.focus: Make a one-page decision tree for integrals: form of integrand to technique. Then verify the tree against every problem on both exams.

lessons.title: Final: Series, Convergence, and the Infinite

notes.summary: The calculus finale: series comparison tests (the video), improper integrals, and Taylor approximations all in one exam. Work the official final under exam conditions, then close the loop by writing a one-page synthesis of the entire two-term arc: rate of change to accumulation to approximation. Next term, linear algebra replaces the single variable with systems.
concepts: Comparison and ratio intuition for series
notes.focus: Before opening the exam, write the course map from memory: limits, derivatives, applications, integrals, techniques, series. The gaps in your map are exactly what to review tonight.
